challenges.judge_assessment: The brief asserts that liability reaches all appellees without distinguishing among Lake Shore Towers, Showe Management, 609 Walnut Limited Partnership, and Ball. It does not identify which entity employed each person, which entity owned or possessed the table, or which entity controlled the allegedly negligent activity. Proximate cause requires a reasonable connection between a particular defendant's act or omission and the injury. Even if some negligence issue existed, the brief has not justified reversal as to every appellee or shown a basis for imposing undifferentiated liability on separate defendants.
challenges.suggested_response: Because appellees have not distinguished among the respective roles of the corporate defendants and Ball in the summary-judgment record, the court cannot conclude as a matter of law that any one appellee is free from liability. At minimum, the testimony creates a genuine issue whether the corporate appellees, through the employees who controlled the storage room and arranged appellant's access to it, bear responsibility for the condition that caused appellant's injuries.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Do not say liability necessarily reaches all appellees unless the brief can separate the defendants by role and evidence. The argument should be narrowed to the corporate appellees whose employees controlled the room, or else the brief needs record support distinguishing each entity's involvement.

attacks_proposed.argument: The brief treats res judicata and lack of negligence evidence as though defeating either ground requires reversal. But where summary judgment rests on independently sufficient grounds, appellant must demonstrate error as to each; judgment remains proper if either res judicata bars the action or the Civ.R. 56 evidence fails to establish an actionable negligence claim. Ohio's summary-judgment framework imposes a reciprocal burden on the nonmovant to identify specific facts creating a genuine issue once the movant satisfies its initial burden. [55]
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Unless appellant defeats every independently sufficient basis for judgment, reversal does not follow even if one argument succeeds.

attacks_proposed.argument: The assertion that Civ.R. 1(C) categorically removes forcible-entry-and-detainer proceedings from all Civil Rules is overbroad. Ohio authority applies Civil Rules that are not clearly inapplicable to such proceedings, while disregarding only rules whose nature would frustrate the statutory summary process. [11,16] More specifically, the compulsory-counterclaim exception identified in the landlord-tenant authority applies when the eviction complaint alleges only possession. [2] The brief itself acknowledges a separate 2004 action for back rent and breach of lease, so the possession-only exception does not resolve the preclusive effect of that action.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: The brief's principal legal premise does not dispose of the 2004 back-rent action, where ordinary compulsory-counterclaim principles may apply.

attacks_proposed.argument: The addition of 609 Walnut Limited Partnership and Ball as defendants does not, without more, establish that appellant's own claim against the prior opposing parties was noncompulsory. The cited Ohio material distinguishes claims belonging to a person who was not a party to the eviction—such as a nonparty child's own claim—from claims belonging to the tenant who was already a party. [4] The brief supplies no Civ.R. 56 evidence or jurisdictional analysis supporting its bare assertion that Ball could not have been joined, and unsupported allegations do not satisfy the nonmovant's reciprocal summary-judgment burden. [55]
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Even if claims against genuinely new parties survive, appellant has not shown why claim preclusion could not still protect parties to the prior action or otherwise support judgment in part.

attacks_proposed.argument: The brief declares that the injury claim was not logically related to the 2004 back-rent and breach-of-lease action without presenting the earlier pleadings, lease claims, judgment, or other Civ.R. 56 material needed to compare the transactions. The possession-only rule does not answer this question, [2] and Ohio landlord-tenant materials recognize that rent and tenant claims can carry compulsory-counterclaim consequences when they overlap. [22] A conclusory assertion of no logical relationship is not a substitute for specific facts under the reciprocal Civ.R. 56 burden. [55]
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Without the contents of the 2004 action, appellant cannot establish that the trial court erred in treating the personal-injury claim as arising from the same tenancy-related controversy.

attacks_proposed.argument: An invitation into the room and management's control of it may address appellant's lawful presence, but they do not themselves prove breach, notice of a dangerous condition, or causation. Ohio premises-liability law recognizes no duty to protect a lawful entrant from an open and obvious danger, [40] and a negligence claimant must establish a reasonable causal connection between a defendant's act or omission and the injury. [63] The brief identifies no evidence that any appellee knew or should have known the table was unstable, how long any unsafe placement existed, or what act made it fall.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Invitee status alone cannot create a triable negligence claim; failure of breach, notice, or causation independently supports summary judgment.

attacks_proposed.argument: Res ipsa loquitur is not established merely because appellees controlled the room. The brief's own formulation requires exclusive control of the injury-causing instrumentality and circumstances showing the accident would not have occurred with ordinary care. Yet the evidence described places appellant and multiple persons in the room, says only that the table either fell or was knocked over, and never identifies what destabilized it. Later use of the table in the ballroom does not establish exclusive control at the relevant time. Nor does the circular statement that ordinary care would have prevented the injury supply the required causal connection between an appellee's act or omission and the accident. [63] Conclusory assertions cannot satisfy the nonmovant's Civ.R. 56 burden. [55]
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Without evidence satisfying both res ipsa elements, the doctrine cannot fill the admitted evidentiary gap concerning breach and causation.

attacks_proposed.argument: The brief incorrectly frames open and obvious danger as requiring proof that appellant actually recognized the danger, voluntarily encountered it, and was personally at fault. Ohio's rule is objective: a landowner owes no duty as to dangers known to the entrant or so obvious and apparent that the entrant may reasonably be expected to discover them. [40] The relevant condition is not an abstract folding table but the visible placement of a six-foot table leaning in the storage room. The brief itself recounts appellant noticing the table and being told not to touch it, yet it does not analyze whether the table's placement was objectively observable.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the allegedly dangerous placement was objectively open and obvious, appellees owed no common-law premises duty concerning it, regardless of appellant's subjective appreciation or comparative fault.

attacks_proposed.argument: The contention that a six-foot folding table cannot be a dangerous condition addresses the wrong question and undercuts appellant's own negligence theory. The alleged danger is the manner in which the table was positioned or handled, not the table's generic character. Open-and-obvious analysis asks whether the condition was sufficiently apparent that an entrant could reasonably be expected to discover it. [40] The brief cannot establish breach by calling the placement hazardous while avoiding the duty defense by describing the same condition merely as a harmless table.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: A proper focus on the table's placement, rather than the object in isolation, preserves the open-and-obvious defense and exposes the absence of evidence identifying a negligent act.

attacks_proposed.argument: Respondeat superior does not cure the absence of proof that an employee committed a tort. The brief offers alternatives—improper storage, Ball causing the fall, or some other unidentified employee causing it—but identifies no specific act, actor, or evidence tying that act to the fall. Ohio negligence law still requires a reasonable causal connection between the asserted act or omission and the injury. [63] Moreover, the brief's factual statement identifies ownership, management, and Ball's employment principally as complaint allegations; Civ.R. 56 does not permit the nonmovant to rest on pleading allegations after a properly supported motion. [55]
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Without evidence of an employee's tort, causation, employment relationship, and scope of employment, there is no predicate liability to impute to any corporate appellee.

attacks_proposed.argument: The assertion that liability necessarily reaches all appellees fails to distinguish among Lake Shore Towers, Showe Management, 609 Walnut Limited Partnership, and Ball. The brief does not identify which entity employed each person, which entity owned or possessed the table, or which entity controlled the allegedly negligent activity. Its alternative theory that Ball or another employee must have caused the accident is speculation rather than a specific fact showing a genuine issue. [55] Proximate cause requires a reasonable connection between a particular defendant's act or omission and the injury. [63]
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Even if some negligence issue existed, the brief has not justified reversal as to every appellee or shown a basis for imposing undifferentiated liability on separate defendants.

judge_assessments.assessment: The brief argues that the personal injury claim could not have been a compulsory counterclaim because two defendants were not parties to the forcible entry and detainer action. That argument does not address whether the claim against the defendants who were parties to the prior action is barred. The cited authority distinguishes claims belonging to a nonparty from claims belonging to a party, and the brief offers no Civ.R. 56 evidence or jurisdictional analysis to show that the claim against the existing parties could not have been brought. This gap leaves the res judicata defense partially intact.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: First and most importantly, appellant's personal injury claim in this case could not have been brought as a compulsory counterclaim in the forcible entry and detainer action because the parties to the above case are different. Specifically, appellant filed this lawsuit against Lakeshore Towers, Inc., Showe Management Corp., 609 Walnut Limited Partnership, and Marie Ball. Neither 609 Walnut Limited Partnership, nor Ms. Ball was a party in the forcible entry detainer action. Civ.R. 13(A) specifically excludes as compulsory counterclaims any claim which would be brought against third parties to which the court would not have jurisdiction. Ms. Ball, as an employee of the apartment building, could not have been named a party in the 2003 forcible entry and detainer action.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Research whether Ohio law permits a compulsory counterclaim against only some of the prior parties and whether the presence of new defendants defeats claim preclusion as to the original parties.

judge_assessments.assessment: The brief asserts that the personal injury claim was not logically related to the 2004 back-rent and breach-of-lease action, but it provides no pleadings, lease terms, judgment, or other Civ.R. 56 material from that action. Without that record, the court cannot compare the transactions to determine whether they arise from the same controversy. The possession-only rule does not resolve the preclusive effect of a back-rent action, and Ohio authority recognizes that rent and tenant claims can be compulsory when they overlap. A conclusory assertion of no logical relationship does not satisfy the nonmovant's reciprocal burden under Civ.R. 56.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: Here, even though there was a 2004 action for back rent, appellant's claim was still not a compulsory counterclaim because, as discussed above, it is not logically related to the action for back rent. Most notably, unlike in Sherman, supra, the injury here did not occur in a common area.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Obtain the record of the 2004 back-rent action to assess whether the personal injury claim arises from the same transaction or occurrence under the Rettig logical-relation test.

judge_assessments.assessment: The brief invokes res ipsa loquitur but does not establish either element with specific facts. The evidence shows multiple people in the room and that the table either fell or was knocked over, without identifying what destabilized it. The later use of the table in the ballroom does not demonstrate exclusive control at the time of the accident. The statement that ordinary care would have prevented the injury is circular and does not supply the required causal connection between an appellee's act or omission and the accident. Conclusory assertions cannot satisfy the nonmovant's Civ.R. 56 burden.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: It is clear from the appellees' own testimony that the storage room where appellant suffered his injury was under their exclusive control. ... Second, appellant did not cause this injury to himself, and had the appellees exercised ordinary care, appellant would not have been injured.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Review Ohio case law on res ipsa loquitur in premises liability cases involving falling objects to determine whether exclusive control and the inference of negligence can be established on similar facts.

judge_assessments.assessment: The brief misstates the open-and-obvious doctrine by requiring proof that the plaintiff actually recognized the danger and voluntarily encountered it. Ohio law applies an objective standard: a landowner owes no duty as to dangers that are known to the entrant or so obvious and apparent that the entrant may reasonably be expected to discover them. The brief's own account shows appellant noticed the table and was told not to touch it, yet it does not analyze whether the table's placement was objectively observable. This error undermines the argument that the doctrine does not apply.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: First, in order for this doctrine to apply, the plaintiff must be at some fault for his conduct; the plaintiff must have recognized the dangerous condition and still chosen to encounter it. Appellant did not encounter the folding table that knocked him to the ground and unconscious. The folding table struck him.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Confirm the current Ohio Supreme Court articulation of the open-and-obvious doctrine, particularly in premises liability cases involving movable objects.

judge_assessments.assessment: The brief argues that a six-foot folding table cannot be a dangerous condition as a matter of law, but the alleged danger is the manner in which the table was positioned or handled, not the table's generic character. The open-and-obvious analysis focuses on whether the condition was sufficiently apparent. By characterizing the table as harmless while simultaneously claiming its placement was hazardous, the brief creates an internal inconsistency that weakens both the negligence theory and the response to the open-and-obvious defense.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: As a matter of law, nobody can claim that a six (6) foot long folding table is a 'dangerous condition.' Climbing electric fences; walking into gaping holes in the street; walking on wet floors in a shopping center that have been properly marked; these are examples of the 'open and obvious' doctrine absolving property owners of their liability.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Examine Ohio appellate decisions applying the open-and-obvious doctrine to falling or unstable objects to see whether the object's generic character or its specific placement controls.

judge_assessments.assessment: The brief invokes respondeat superior but identifies no specific act, actor, or evidence tying any employee's conduct to the table falling. The alternatives offered—improper storage, Ball causing the fall, or another employee causing it—are speculation. Ohio negligence law requires a reasonable causal connection between the asserted act or omission and the injury. Moreover, the brief's factual statements about employment relationships rely on complaint allegations, which cannot substitute for Civ.R. 56 evidence after a properly supported motion. Without proof of an employee's tort, causation, and scope of employment, there is no predicate liability to impute to any corporate appellee.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: Either the table fell on appellant because it was improperly stored, or a specific appellee, caused the table to fall upon him. Under either of those scenarios, liability flows to the corporate Lakeshore Towers, Inc. through the doctrine of respondeat superior.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Review the summary judgment record for any deposition testimony or interrogatory answers identifying who moved or placed the table and whether that person was acting within the scope of employment.

judge_assessments.assessment: The brief asserts that liability reaches all appellees without distinguishing among Lake Shore Towers, Showe Management, 609 Walnut Limited Partnership, and Ball. It does not identify which entity employed each person, which entity owned or possessed the table, or which entity controlled the allegedly negligent activity. Proximate cause requires a reasonable connection between a particular defendant's act or omission and the injury. Even if some negligence issue existed, the brief has not justified reversal as to every appellee or shown a basis for imposing undifferentiated liability on separate defendants.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: In this case, it is clear that the tort committed upon appellant was caused either directly by Maric Ball or through another employee of Lakeshore Towers acting within the course and scope of their employment. Therefore, appellant is entitled to present this evidence to a jury as to appellees' negligence.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Determine whether the record contains evidence of the corporate structure, employment relationships, and control over the storage room and table sufficient to link each defendant to the alleged negligence.

results.assessment: The brief has a workable overall narrative, especially that the accident should go to a jury and that appellees overstate their defenses, but as written it is vulnerable on several core points. Its res judicata answer is conclusory because it lacks the prior pleadings, lease terms, and judgment needed to show the 2004 action was not a compulsory counterclaim issue. Its res ipsa and respondeat superior sections also lean on speculation without identifying a specific actor, act, or exclusive control at the critical time. The open-and-obvious discussion is misstated by using a subjective lens instead of the objective one. The research does not resolve the missing summary-judgment record.

elements.label: A notice to leave the premises was served
elements.requirement: The brief identifies a notice and says it was served on the tenant.
elements.explanation: The brief, through its cited Amick discussion, states that notice to vacate was left at the premises and treated as served. That is enough to plead service and the supplied excerpt supports it.
elements.quote: "It is undisputed that appellee left a notice to vacate at the premises. It is also undisputed that the notice was served on December 23, 2006, and that the complaint was not filed until December 29, six days later."

elements.label: The notice carried the language the statute requires
elements.requirement: The brief says whether the notice contained the statutorily required language, and quotes or attaches it rather than characterizing it.
elements.explanation: The brief never quotes or attaches the actual notice text to show it used the statutory form. It discusses notice requirements in the abstract, but that is not the same as showing the notice contained the required language.

elements.label: The notice was served by a permitted method
elements.requirement: The brief names how the notice was delivered.
elements.explanation: The brief identifies service by leaving the notice at the premises, which is a permitted method. The supplied excerpt also quotes the statute’s authorized delivery methods.
elements.quote: "R.C. 1923.04(A), 'a party desiring to commence an action under this chapter shall notify the adverse party to leave the premises... three or more days before beginning the action, by certified mail, return receipt requested, or by handing a written copy of the notice to the defendant in person, or by leaving it at the defendant's usual place of abode or at the premises from which the defendant is sought to be evicted.'"

elements.label: The statutory period ran before the complaint was filed
elements.requirement: The brief gives both the service date and the filing date, so the period between them can be counted rather than assumed.
elements.explanation: The brief gives both the service date and the filing date, so the interval can be counted directly. The excerpt says the notice was served on December 23 and the complaint was filed on December 29, six days later.

challenges.opponent_argument: The brief treats nonpayment of cash rent as dispositive, but R.C. 5321.01(A) defines a tenant by entitlement under a rental agreement, not by a freestanding cash-rent requirement. Ohio landlord-tenant authority also recognizes that an employee may lease residential premises pursuant to a contract of employment. Thus, the necessary inquiry is whether the employment arrangement itself established terms governing Lee's use and occupancy of the room; the absence of a separate written lease or payroll deduction does not answer that question. [41, 4]
challenges.why_it_matters: If the employment arrangement could constitute an oral rental agreement or employee tenancy, the brief has not established the absence of tenancy as a matter of law, and summary judgment on that premise cannot stand.

challenges.judge_assessment: The brief's rule that absence of cash rent and separate lease precludes tenancy ignores the statutory definition and the recognized employee-tenant category. The cited authority (source 4) indicates that an employment contract may constitute a rental agreement, and consideration need not be cash. The brief does not address this, so its categorical conclusion is vulnerable.
challenges.suggested_response: The dispositive question is whether Appellant was "entitled under a rental agreement to the use and occupancy of residential premises to the exclusion of others." R.C. 5321.01(A). The trial court found there was no rental agreement and no rent was paid, and Appellant has not pointed to competent evidence that the employment arrangement itself created a rental agreement or leasehold. On this record, the employee-tenant authorities do not change the result, because they require some agreement conferring a possessory right, not merely occupancy in connection with employment.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Narrow the tenancy analysis to the statutory definition and the trial court’s actual findings. Do not say the absence of cash rent alone is dispositive; instead, say Appellant failed to show an entitlement under a rental agreement to occupy the premises.

challenges.opponent_argument: The categorical statement that anyone living with another "for whatever purpose" without rent is not a tenant overlooks the recognized employee-tenant category. Ohio authority states that an employee may lease and reside in residential premises pursuant to a contract of employment and that Chapter 5321 modified the common-law treatment of employee tenants. The purpose and terms of the occupancy therefore matter; employment-related occupancy cannot be collapsed automatically into social-guest occupancy. [4]
challenges.why_it_matters: Ogle and Stone, as characterized in the brief, involved social or domestic co-occupants. Without addressing the legally distinct employee-tenant framework, those cases do not conclusively resolve Lee's status.

The record before the trial court showed no rental agreement and no rent paid, so Appellant’s wrongful-eviction counts, which depend on tenancy, fail as a matter of law.

However, Amick involved an FED action; the court held that the 30-day notice under R.C. 5321.17 did not apply, but the FED action proceeded. Amick does not support the claim that self-help is permissible. This misreading undermines a key authority.
challenges.suggested_response: Amick supports Appellees only for the limited point that where the occupant is not a tenant, tenant-specific notice provisions such as R.C. 5321.17 do not control. Appellees do not cite Amick as authority for a free-standing right of self-help; rather, they cite it to show that Appellant cannot convert a non-tenancy into a wrongful-eviction claim by invoking statutes that presuppose a tenancy.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Stop using Amick as if it approved self-help. Use it only for the limited proposition that tenant-specific notice rules do not apply when the occupant is not a tenant.

challenges.opponent_argument: R.C. 5321.15(A)'s focus on residential tenants does not establish the converse proposition that every non-tenant may be removed through self-help. record_sources.quote: "Section 5321.15(A) provides that landlords may only evict residential tenants by following the procedures set forth in Chapters 1923, 5303, and 5321 of the Ohio Revised Code."

challenges.judge_assessment: The brief argues that because R.C. 5321.15(A) makes FED exclusive only for residential tenants, Appellees were free to use self-help. However, the absence of a statutory tenant remedy does not automatically make self-help lawful. The brief provides no affirmative authority permitting self-help against this type of occupier. This gap is critical.
challenges.suggested_response: R.C. 5321.15(A) is directed to landlords recovering possession from tenants. It does not supply Appellant with a wrongful-eviction claim absent a tenancy, and Appellant cites no Ohio authority extending that statute to a person who is not entitled under a rental agreement to occupy the premises. The issue is therefore not whether FED was available to Appellees in the abstract, but whether Appellant can satisfy the tenant-based elements of her claims. She cannot on this record.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Remove the leap from non-tenant status to lawful self-help. Make the argument only that Appellant’s tenant-based statutes do not create liability absent a tenancy, and that she cites no authority extending those statutes here.

challenges.opponent_argument: R.C. 1923.02(A)'s statement that proceedings "may be had" identifies when an FED action is available; it does not affirmatively authorize unilateral self-help. The same statute expressly reaches categories beyond statutory tenants, including persons subject to the listed possession proceedings. Reading "may" as permission to bypass judicial process confuses authorization to bring an action with authorization to recover possession without one. [22]
challenges.why_it_matters: If "may" merely confers an available summary remedy, the brief loses its principal textual basis for claiming that self-help was lawful.

challenges.judge_assessment: The brief reads "may be had" in R.C. 1923.02(A) as permission to bypass judicial process entirely. The statute's permissive language merely indicates that FED proceedings are available; it does not affirmatively authorize self-help. The brief's leap from "not mandatory" to "self-help permitted" lacks supporting authority.
challenges.suggested_response: R.C. 1923.02(A) identifies the classes of cases in which FED proceedings may be brought; it does not speak to Appellant’s status as a tenant, and it does not create a wrongful-eviction claim for a person who lacks a rental agreement. Appellant’s reliance on the statute therefore does not answer the dispositive question here: whether she was entitled under a rental agreement to the use and occupancy of the premises. The trial court correctly held she was not.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Correct the statutory-reading point. Do not say "may be had" means self-help is permitted; say only that R.C. 1923.02(A) identifies when FED proceedings are available.

challenges.opponent_argument: The commercial-lease authorities do not establish a general self-help rule for residential employee housing. As the brief itself describes them, those decisions concern commercial premises and repossession under voluntarily negotiated self-help provisions, including limitations involving absence of a breach of the peace and acquiescence. Residential lockouts are governed by a distinct statutory framework that prohibits specified self-help conduct against tenants. [38, 41]
challenges.why_it_matters: Removing the commercial cases from the analysis leaves no cited authority extending commercial contractual self-help principles to a disputed residential employment-accommodation arrangement.

results.assessment: The brief has a workable core if the record truly shows no rental agreement and no rent: on that footing, it can argue Appellant did not satisfy the tenant-based statutes she invokes. But as written it is exposed by several overstatements that need fixing. It treats the absence of cash rent and a separate lease as dispositive, even though Ohio authority recognizes that employment-related occupancy can still create a rental agreement or tenancy. It also misreads Amick and stretches commercial self-help cases into the residential setting. The R.C. 1923.02(A) "may be had" language does not itself authorize self-help, so the brief should stop implying it does. The research did not settle whether the employment arrangement here actually created a possessory right.

challenges.opponent_argument: The argument incorrectly converts the word “may” in R.C. 1923.02 into affirmative permission to use self-help. The statute expressly makes Chapter 1923 proceedings available against both holdover tenants and other occupiers, while R.C. 1923.01 addresses unlawful or forcible entry and unlawful detention. Saying that an FED action “may be had” identifies the persons subject to that statutory proceeding; it does not identify every lawful extrajudicial means of dispossession or immunize forcible removal. [21, 23]
challenges.why_it_matters: Even if Chapter 1923 is not textually labeled the exclusive remedy for every occupant, Appellees still need authority establishing that the particular self-help used here was lawful. The cited statutory language alone does not supply that authority.

Amick involved a judicial eviction, not self-help. The brief's inference that these cases permit self-help is unsupported.
challenges.suggested_response: Ogle, Stone, and Amick support the narrower and dispositive point that a person who occupies premises without a rental agreement and without paying rent is not a tenant under Chapter 5321. Those cases do not hold that every non-tenant occupant must be removed by FED, and Amick is distinguishable because it involved a judicial eviction after notice, not approval of self-help removal.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Use Ogle, Stone, and Amick only for the narrower proposition that a rent-free occupant without a rental agreement is not a Chapter 5321 tenant. Do not suggest those cases approved self-help; acknowledge that Amick proceeded by judicial eviction and therefore does not decide whether self-help is lawful.

challenges.judge_assessment: The brief's broad assertion that all live-in employees can be removed without FED when no cash rent is paid is unsupported. Ohio law recognizes employee tenants, and the analysis must be agreement-specific. The brief's categorical rule is not grounded in cited authority.
challenges.suggested_response: Ohio law recognizes that an employee may, in some circumstances, lease and reside in residential premises pursuant to a contract of employment. But that principle is agreement-specific. It does not create a categorical rule that every live-in caregiver or other employee may be removed without FED whenever no cash rent is paid. Appellant has identified no evidence that her arrangement created a rental agreement or any other possessory right under Chapter 5321.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Concede that Ohio recognizes employee tenants in some circumstances, but make clear that employee status alone is not enough. The brief should say the analysis is agreement-specific and that Appellant has not identified evidence of an employment contract or other arrangement creating a rental agreement or possessory right.

attacks_proposed.argument: The brief treats payment of cash rent as indispensable to tenant status, but R.C. 5321.01(A) asks whether the occupant was entitled to use and occupancy under a rental agreement; it does not separately require cash rent. A rental agreement may be written or oral and may establish terms concerning occupancy, and Ohio landlord-tenant materials specifically recognize that an employee may lease residential premises pursuant to an employment contract. Thus, the dispositive question is whether Lee's required overnight service and furnished room formed an occupancy agreement supported by her labor, not merely whether money was labeled or withheld as rent. [8, 54, 2]
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If employment services could supply the consideration or terms of an oral rental agreement, the absence of cash rent does not establish non-tenant status as a matter of law, and summary judgment cannot rest on that categorical premise.

attacks_proposed.argument: The supplied record does not substantiate the Lee-specific facts on which the conclusion depends: that no oral occupancy agreement existed, that the room was merely an on-duty accommodation, that no compensation was allocated to lodging, and that her occupancy lacked exclusivity. The supplied material establishes only what occurred in Ogle, Stone, and Amick; it contains no deposition or employment evidence concerning Lee. [upload:47]
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Without record evidence eliminating an oral employment-based occupancy agreement, Appellees have not shown the absence of a genuine factual issue on the element that determines tenant status.

attacks_proposed.argument: The argument incorrectly converts the word “may” in R.C. 1923.02 into affirmative permission to use self-help. The statute expressly makes Chapter 1923 proceedings available against both holdover tenants and other occupiers, while R.C. 1923.01 addresses unlawful or forcible entry and unlawful detention. Saying that an FED action “may be had” identifies the persons subject to that statutory proceeding; it does not identify every lawful extrajudicial means of dispossession or immunize forcible removal. [21, 23]
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Even if Chapter 1923 is not textually labeled the exclusive remedy for every occupant, Appellees still need authority establishing that the particular self-help used here was lawful. The cited statutory language alone does not supply that authority.

attacks_proposed.argument: Ogle, Stone, and Amick support the narrower proposition that a rent-free cohabitant without a rental agreement is not protected as a Chapter 5321 tenant. They do not establish the separate proposition that an owner may remove every non-tenant residential occupant through self-help. Amick is especially unhelpful on that step because the owner actually pursued an FED action, served R.C. 1923.04 notice, and obtained a judicial eviction; the decision upheld that procedure rather than approving removal without process. [39, 42; upload:47]
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: The authorities may defeat a Chapter 5321 theory if Lee was conclusively a non-tenant, but they do not prove the brief's central remedial inference that self-help was lawful and FED unnecessary.

attacks_proposed.argument: The commercial-lease analogy does not establish a general residential self-help rule. The authority quoted by the brief itself addresses a negotiated commercial lease containing a self-help provision and conditions its conclusion on repossession without breach of the peace and with the lessee's acquiescence. The brief identifies no comparable self-help agreement or established acquiescence here. Moreover, R.C. 1923.02 expressly provides an FED procedure for occupiers without color of title. [23]
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Northfield's limited commercial holding cannot carry the much broader conclusion that a residential caregiver may be summarily removed absent an agreed self-help provision and the factual safeguards emphasized in that authority.

attacks_proposed.argument: The inapplicability of R.C. 5321.15(A) would mean only that Lee lacks the statutory remedy reserved to a tenant against a landlord. It does not follow that every manner of removal was lawful or that all wrongful-removal theories fail. R.C. 5321.15(C)'s damages remedy is tied to a violation of subsection (A), but nothing in the cited material turns failure to qualify for that remedy into blanket immunity from other claims. Ohio authority also recognizes punitive consequences for self-help eviction contrary to statutory regulation. [27, 35]
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: The trial court could not dispose of every challenged count merely by deciding Lee was not a statutory tenant unless Appellees also demonstrated that each count depended exclusively on R.C. 5321.15 and that no independent wrongful conduct remained at issue.

attacks_proposed.argument: Lee's maintenance of another mailing address or backup room does not resolve the statutory question. R.C. 5321.01(A) turns on entitlement under a rental agreement to use and occupy residential premises to the exclusion of others, not on driver's-license address, voter registration, or whether the occupant maintained another possible residence. [8]
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Those address facts cannot substitute for analysis of the parties' actual employment and occupancy agreement and therefore cannot independently support summary judgment on tenant status.

attacks_proposed.argument: The sweeping assertion that live-in nurses, caregivers, nannies, clergy, boarding-school workers, and numerous other employees may always be removed without FED whenever no cash rent is paid is unsupported. Ohio landlord-tenant materials recognize an “employee tenant” whose right to reside arises under a contract of employment and explain that Chapter 5321 modified the common-law treatment of employee occupancy. The required analysis is therefore agreement-specific, not occupationally categorical. [2]
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: The court cannot affirm on the proposed universal rule for employee occupants; it must determine what occupancy rights this employment arrangement actually created.

attacks_proposed.argument: The policy argument that immediate self-help is necessary because FED would disrupt families and businesses overlooks that Ohio characterizes FED as a summary, extraordinary, and speedy remedy designed to resolve possession promptly. That statutory design weakens the claimed need to infer an uncodified right of immediate residential self-help. [72]
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Administrative convenience and urgency do not justify expanding commercial self-help principles beyond their stated limits when Ohio already supplies an expedited judicial possession remedy.

attacks_proposed.argument: The brief's distinction of Reynolds as involving an alleged lifetime lease does not answer the potentially relevant principle: compensation for live-in nursing or housekeeping services may form part of an agreement granting residential occupancy. Ohio materials expressly recognize that an employment contract can also provide an employee with leased residential premises. Merely labeling Reynolds procedurally different therefore does not eliminate its relevance to whether Lee's services could support an occupancy agreement. [2, 54]
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If services rather than cash could support the alleged right of occupancy, the brief cannot establish the absence of a rental agreement solely through the absence of conventional rent.

judge_assessments.assessment: The brief's categorical reliance on absence of cash rent and written rental agreement overlooks that R.C. 5321.01(A) defines tenant by entitlement under a rental agreement, which can be oral and can arise from an employment contract. Ohio authority recognizes employee tenants. The brief does not address whether Lee's services and the provided room could constitute an oral rental agreement. This gap undermines the summary judgment on tenant status.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief asserts no oral or written rental agreement existed and no rent was paid, but does not discuss whether the employment arrangement itself could be a rental agreement.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Further research into Ohio case law on employee tenants and whether services can constitute consideration for a rental agreement would clarify.

judge_assessments.assessment: The brief's reading of R.C. 1923.02's 'may' as permissive does not establish that self-help eviction is lawful. The statute identifies who may be subject to FED proceedings, but does not authorize extrajudicial removal. The brief provides no affirmative authority for the self-help used here.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief argues that because FED is not mandatory for non-tenants, Appellees were not limited to FED. It does not cite authority permitting self-help.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Research on Ohio common law regarding self-help eviction of non-tenant occupants would be needed.

judge_assessments.assessment: Ogle, Stone, and Amick support that a rent-free occupant without a rental agreement is not a Chapter 5321 tenant, but they do not hold that self-help removal is lawful. Amick involved a judicial eviction, not self-help. The brief's inference that these cases permit self-help is unsupported.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief cites these cases to show that without tenancy, FED is not the exclusive remedy, implying self-help is allowed. It does not acknowledge that Amick used FED.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Examination of whether any Ohio case has extended these holdings to approve self-help would be necessary.

judge_assessments.assessment: The commercial-lease analogy from Northfield is inapposite. That case involved a negotiated self-help clause and no breach of peace. The brief does not identify any similar agreement or acquiescence here. Extending that holding to a residential caregiver without a self-help provision is a significant leap.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief quotes Northfield to argue that outside residential tenancy, FED is not exclusive, but does not address the factual limitations of that case.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Research on whether Ohio courts have applied Northfield to residential non-tenant situations would clarify.

judge_assessments.assessment: The brief's broad assertion that all live-in employees can be removed without FED when no cash rent is paid is unsupported. Ohio law recognizes employee tenants, and the analysis must be agreement-specific. The brief's categorical rule is not grounded in cited authority.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief states in u139 that various employee types can be removed without FED absent a rental agreement and rent. It does not cite authority for this proposition beyond the general non-tenant cases.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Research on Ohio treatment of employee tenants and whether any case has adopted such a categorical rule would be needed.

results.assessment: The brief is strongest where it insists Appellant identified no evidence of a rental agreement or protected possessory interest, and where it uses the cited cases only for the narrower point that a rent-free occupant without such an agreement is not a Chapter 5321 tenant. Its main weakness is that it still does not squarely answer whether self-help removal was lawful against a non-tenant occupant, and several passages overstate the rule by sounding categorical about cash rent and live-in employees. The research did not settle any affirmative authority for self-help, so the brief should avoid implying more than the cited materials support.

attacks_proposed.argument: Plaintiff cannot obtain summary judgment based on evidence merely described as “to be presented.” Civ.R. 56 requires the court to decide the motion from the permissible materials presently in the record, and the Civil Rules apply to forcible-entry proceedings unless clearly inapplicable. The motion therefore succeeds only to the extent its currently submitted materials establish every element. [41]
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Any essential proposition depending on anticipated rather than filed evidence—particularly title, deed delivery, or the right to present possession—cannot support judgment now.

attacks_proposed.argument: The evidence shows execution of a quitclaim deed, but the supplied record does not establish delivery of that deed to the Estate or even the asserted delivery to the probate court. Plaintiff's own rule makes proper execution and delivery necessary to pass title; the principle that recording is unnecessary does not eliminate the separate delivery requirement. The authority addressing title issues likewise recognizes that an unrecorded deed may pass title, not that execution alone necessarily does so. [4]
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Without proof of delivery, plaintiff has not conclusively established that the deed transferred present title, which is the foundation of its claimed superior right to possession.

attacks_proposed.argument: The probate entry quoted in the record orders that 8127 Cedar Road “be transferred” to the Estate; it does not itself say that title is presently divested from defendants and vested in the Estate. Plaintiff identifies no evidence or authority establishing that this directive, standing alone, completed the conveyance. Because the deed-delivery evidence is also absent, the order and executed deed do not conclusively establish the completed transfer plaintiff asserts.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: A directive to make a future transfer is not necessarily proof that the transfer was completed. That evidentiary gap prevents plaintiff from establishing present title as a matter of law.

attacks_proposed.argument: Plaintiff cannot satisfy R.C. 1923.02(A)(5) merely by asserting that defendants have produced no proof of color of title. The statute requires an occupier without color of title and a complainant with the right of possession. [2] Under the summary-judgment burden stated in plaintiff's own materials, the movant must first identify evidence demonstrating the absence of a genuine dispute on each essential issue; only then does the response burden shift. The notice's statement that defendants occupy “without color of title” is plaintiff's own allegation and does not independently prove its truth. Evidence rules apply in forcible-entry actions, and hearsay generally is inadmissible. [42]
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Unless plaintiff first proves present title and the absence of any continuing colorable interest, defendants' supposed lack of contrary proof cannot itself justify summary judgment.

attacks_proposed.argument: The March 2023 probate entry establishes authority to manage the properties— including inventorying, collecting rents, paying taxes, making repairs, and insuring buildings—but the quoted language does not expressly award plaintiff exclusive possession or direct defendants' eviction. Because present possession may depend on present ownership, management authority cannot cure the unresolved proof of deed delivery and completed title transfer. [4]
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: The management order is not an independent substitute for proof that plaintiff presently holds the superior possessory interest required for relief under R.C. 1923.02(A)(5).

attacks_proposed.argument: The assertions that Gino transferred “all” property he could find and that the property was worth approximately $2 million exceed the supplied evidence. The record supports transfers of identified real properties, including 8127 Cedar Road, but does not establish the asserted total value or a transfer of every asset.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Those unsupported allegations should be disregarded and cannot be used to strengthen the inference that the present possession claim is undisputed. They do not replace proof of the elements of the statutory claim.

attacks_proposed.argument: The record supports continued occupancy, but it does not establish the additional assertions that defendants refused to remove their belongings or that the Estate lacks access by key. Those assertions therefore cannot be treated as undisputed Civ.R. 56 facts.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: The court should not rely on these unsupported circumstances when deciding entitlement to immediate restitution. The motion must stand on admissible proof of title, present possession, and statutory compliance rather than unproved allegations about access or belongings.

results.assessment: The motion has a usable summary-judgment structure and the procedural Civ.R. 56 attack is not fatal by itself, because the court can disregard any future-proofing language and look only at the present record. But the brief is exposed on the issues that matter most: the record as supplied does not clearly show delivery of the quitclaim deed, so title may not have passed as the motion assumes, and the notice-to-leave showing is incomplete because the permitted method of service is not identified. The three-day waiting-period point is also vulnerable if the filing date is not independently established in the record.

results.assessment: The brief has a workable structure and the probate-order/deed narrative gives it some force on possession, but it is exposed on the points that matter most. It does not affirmatively prove Defendants were without color of title, and it also assumes deed delivery without record support beyond execution and a transfer directive. Those are the core weaknesses. The notice arguments are weaker than the title issues but still under-supported, because the supplied excerpts do not clearly show the certified-mail method or enough detail to remove doubt about strict compliance. The research leaves open whether the attached exhibits cure the notice problem, but it does not cure the missing affirmative proof on title and delivery.

rule_audit.summary: A residential landlord owes statutory duties including compliance with building, housing, health, and safety codes and keeping the premises in a fit and habitable condition. challenges.opponent_argument: The existence of a prior eviction judgment does not itself establish claim preclusion. R.C. 1923.03 provides that judgments under the forcible-entry-and-detainer chapter do not bar later actions by either party. Because the earlier case combined possession and monetary claims, Baker must identify the preclusive effect of the separate damages adjudication rather than treating the eviction proceeding as a whole as automatically barring every later tenancy-related claim.
challenges.why_it_matters: The generic proposition that a final judgment bars claims that could have been litigated does not answer the threshold statutory question whether, and to what extent, this particular mixed eviction action can have preclusive effect.

challenges.judge_assessment: R.C. 1923.03 expressly provides that judgments in forcible entry and detainer actions are not a bar to later actions. The prior municipal court case was brought under that chapter, and the brief does not address this statutory limitation on claim preclusion. This likely defeats the res judicata argument.
challenges.suggested_response: Baker does not rely on the forcible-entry-and-detainer count itself as a bar. The prior municipal case also included a separate monetary claim for back rent and property damage, and the court entered judgment on that claim after hearing evidence. Friese cannot avoid the effect of that final money judgment by invoking the statutory rule applicable to forcible-entry-and-detainer judgments themselves.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Stop treating the prior municipal case as a blanket res judicata bar. If you keep the preclusion theory, distinguish the separately adjudicated money-damages claim from the forcible-entry-and-detainer claim and say the motion relies only on the final judgment on damages.

challenges.opponent_argument: Baker's reliance on R.C. 5321.04(A)(2) addresses only whether the absence of a handrail, by itself, renders a dwelling unfit or uninhabitable. It does not establish the broader proposition that Ohio law imposes no statutory handrail duty. R.C. 5321.04(A)(1) requires compliance with applicable building, housing, health, and safety codes materially affecting health and safety, and the retrieved authority specifically identifies a case applying a city-code duty to install a handrail on a basement stairway.
challenges.why_it_matters: The cited habitability cases do not negate a separate statutory duty arising through an applicable safety or building code, so they cannot establish entitlement to judgment on the entire statutory theory.

challenges.judge_assessment: The brief's argument that no statutory duty exists relies solely on R.C. 5321.04(A)(2) habitability cases. It ignores R.C. 5321.04(A)(1), which requires compliance with applicable building codes, and authority indicates that a handrail requirement may arise from such codes. This leaves a potential statutory duty unaddressed.
challenges.suggested_response: Friese has not identified any applicable building, housing, health, or safety code that required a handrail on this staircase. St. Germain and Taylor address only the limited proposition that the absence of a handrail, standing alone, does not render premises uninhabitable under R.C. 5321.04(A)(2). Baker does not contend that subsection (A)(2) is the only conceivable source of a landlord duty in every case; rather, Friese has pointed to no code-based duty under R.C. 5321.04(A)(1), and the record contains no evidence of a violation.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Narrow the statutory-duty argument. Do not say Ohio law imposes no handrail duty as a categorical matter; say only that Friese has identified no applicable building or safety code that would create a duty under R.C. 5321.04(A)(1) on this record.

challenges.opponent_argument: The open-and-obvious issue cannot be resolved as a matter of law on this record. Although Friese was familiar with the staircase, he also testified that he "really couldn't see the first and second step" and that the available lighting did not fully illuminate the stairwell. Because the doctrine turns on whether the danger itself was discoverable and apparent, this testimony creates a material factual dispute that repeated prior use does not eliminate.
challenges.why_it_matters: If reasonable minds could differ about whether the relevant steps were visible when Friese began descending, Baker cannot obtain summary judgment on the ground that the condition was open and obvious.

challenges.judge_assessment: The brief asserts adequate lighting and familiarity, but Friese's testimony that he could not see the first two steps creates a genuine dispute of material fact as to whether the danger was open and obvious. Summary judgment on this ground is therefore inappropriate.
challenges.suggested_response: Even on Friese’s account, Baker owed no duty to warn of a condition that was actually known to him. Friese testified that he used the basement stairs three to four times each day for nearly four years, that he knew their condition, and that he had told Baker the staircase needed a railing. Under Armstrong, a premises owner has no duty to warn of dangers that are known to the invitee. Friese’s testimony about what he could or could not see at the moment of the fall does not change the undisputed fact that the condition he claims was hazardous—the absence of a railing—was not concealed from him.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Do not rest the open-and-obvious argument on a claim that the stairway was undisputedly well lit. Recast the point around Friese’s actual knowledge of the condition he says made the stairs unsafe—the missing railing—and his repeated daily use of the stairs for years.

challenges.opponent_argument: Baker has not established the required same-transaction-or-occurrence connection merely by observing that both suits relate generally to the tenancy. The prior monetary claim concerned May rent and approximately $5,000 in alleged property damage; the present claim concerns a January fall, the staircase's physical condition, lighting, and the absence of a railing. Those claims depend on materially different conduct, evidence, and injuries. The record supplies no further operative-fact connection between them.

attacks_proposed.argument: The open-and-obvious issue cannot be resolved as a matter of law on this record. Although Friese was familiar with the staircase, he also testified that he "really couldn't see the first and second step" and that the available lighting did not fully illuminate the stairwell. Because the doctrine turns on whether the danger itself was discoverable and apparent, this testimony creates a material factual dispute that repeated prior use does not eliminate.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If reasonable minds could differ about whether the relevant steps were visible when Friese began descending, Baker cannot obtain summary judgment on the ground that the condition was open and obvious.

attacks_proposed.argument: The motion improperly equates Friese's knowledge that no handrail existed with knowledge of the complete danger encountered during the fall. The record also concerns limited visibility of the first two steps and the need to turn from the outward-opening door while beginning the descent. Awareness of one physical feature does not conclusively establish that the danger presented by the stairway under those circumstances was open and obvious.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Baker's no-duty argument succeeds only if the actual condition that caused the risk—not merely the absence of a railing in isolation—was open, apparent, and discoverable.

attacks_proposed.argument: Even if the common-law open-and-obvious doctrine applied to an ordinary premises claim, it would not dispose of any properly established negligence-per-se claim under R.C. 5321.04. Ohio authority recognizes that the doctrine does not apply to statutory claims under R.C. 5321.04(A)(1) or (A)(3). Baker therefore cannot use open and obviousness alone to obtain judgment on the entire complaint while separately placing statutory landlord duties at issue.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: The open-and-obvious defense cannot support complete summary judgment if the evidence permits a statutory landlord-duty theory.

attacks_proposed.argument: Baker's reliance on R.C. 5321.04(A)(2) addresses only whether the absence of a handrail, by itself, renders a dwelling unfit or uninhabitable. R.C. 5321.04(A)(1) requires compliance with applicable building, housing, health, and safety codes materially affecting health and safety, and the retrieved authority specifically identifies a case applying a city-code duty to install a handrail on a basement stairway.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: The cited habitability cases do not negate a separate statutory duty arising through an applicable safety or building code, so they cannot establish entitlement to judgment on the entire statutory theory.

results.verdict: not yet persuasive on the central defenses
results.assessment: The brief has some solid narrowing points: it correctly avoids treating the eviction count alone as the bar, and it usefully limits the handrail cases to the habitability theory. But as written it is exposed on the main issues. It overstates the absence of any handrail duty by not squarely addressing R.C. 5321.04(A)(1) and (A)(3), and the preclusion argument remains vulnerable because the prior money judgment’s service and the same-transaction question are not firmly established. The open-and-obvious argument is also shaky because Friese’s testimony about not seeing the first two steps creates a factual dispute. The research appears adequate; the problem is the brief’s framing, not missing authority.

challenges.judge_assessment: The brief conflates the duty to warn with a duty to install a handrail. The open-and-obvious doctrine eliminates the duty to warn, but does not automatically eliminate an independent statutory duty to provide safe premises, including handrails. The brief's assertion that Baker had no duty to install a handrail is not supported by the open-and-obvious doctrine alone if a statutory duty exists.
challenges.suggested_response: Baker does not dispute that Friese was a business invitee. But an owner of premises is not an insurer of the safety of invitees and owes no common-law duty to warn of dangers that are known to the invitee or so open and obvious that the invitee may reasonably be expected to discover them. Armstrong v. Best Buy Co., Inc., 99 Ohio St.3d 79, 2003-Ohio-2573, ¶ 5. Here, Friese used the basement stairs three to four times a day for nearly four years and testified that he was aware of the condition of the stairway, including that there was no handrail. On that record, Baker had no common-law duty to warn Friese about the stairway condition. To the extent Friese attempts to frame his claim as one under R.C. 5321.04, that issue is addressed separately in the res judicata section below.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Strike or narrow the claim that Baker had no duty to install a handrail based solely on the open-and-obvious doctrine. The better response is that the doctrine eliminates the common-law duty to warn about an open and obvious condition, while any alleged statutory duty must be addressed separately.

challenges.suggested_response: Even if Friese could claim that Baker owed him any kind of duty with regard to the staircase or handrail, his claims for personal injury are barred by res judicata. Under Civ.R. 13(A), a defendant must assert as a compulsory counterclaim any claim arising out of the same transaction or occurrence as the plaintiff's claim, and Ohio courts have applied that rule to tenant personal-injury claims arising from leased premises when the landlord later sues for eviction and monetary damages. Baker's municipal-court action sought both eviction and monetary relief arising out of the tenancy, and judgment was entered on the merits. Friese's present personal-injury claim therefore is barred.
